public_rationale: The January 29, 2025 International AI Safety Report describes uneven capabilities and failures on some simple reasoning tasks [e1]. GPT-4's technical report acknowledges below-human performance in many real-world scenarios and distinguishes pretraining from post-training alignment [e2]. On December 20, 2024, ARC Prize reported that o3 still failed some very easy tasks and judged it not yet AGI [e3]. These findings support the historical claim for the systems covered by this evidence [e1, e2, e3]. The April 13, 2023 version of Sparks reports broad, near-human capabilities in an early GPT-4, but describes it as an incomplete AGI [e4]. That competing assessment does not establish broadly human-level general intelligence produced by pretraining alone [e4].
limitations: The evidence does not establish that future pretraining scaling must fail.
The January synthesis predates the February 18, 2025 claim and cannot establish the capabilities of every system available by that date or of undisclosed private systems.
The training disclosures do not fully isolate pretraining's contribution from other stages.
The evidence supplies neither a universally accepted AGI test nor a basis for treating the word “clearly” as a statement of scientific consensus.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: Pure pretraining scaling has clearly failed to produce AGI.

statement.excerpt: Pure pretraining scaling has clearly failed to produce AGI. 🤷‍♂️

our_interpretation: The present-perfect wording describes what had been achieved by February 18, 2025. It does not establish that future pretraining scaling can never produce AGI.
The plain reading of AGI is broadly human-level general intelligence across cognitive tasks, including adaptation to unfamiliar problems, rather than success on selected benchmarks.

Pure pretraining scaling means increasing pretraining data, model size, and computation; gains requiring additional reasoning training or computation at use time do not demonstrate that pretraining alone sufficed.
The target is the cumulative public record through publication. Its start is unspecified because Marcus names no starting date.
The assessment concerns demonstrated systems, rather than unknowable capabilities of undisclosed private systems.
criteria.support_condition: The public capability record through publication shows that systems developed through scaled pretraining had not demonstrated broadly human-level general intelligence, with contemporary evaluations documenting material gaps.
criteria.contradiction_condition: A system demonstrated by publication meets the ordinary broad human-level standard, with credible training evidence showing that scaling pretraining alone produced that capability.

evidence.locator: Section 1.3.1, discussion of uneven performance; see also section 1.2, Current capabilities
evidence.explanation: The contemporary synthesis documents broad capability gaps, including failures on simple reasoning and inability to independently execute long projects. This supports the inference that broadly human-level general intelligence had not been demonstrated, while the report leaves future scaling disputed.

The developer describes the pretraining method and separately describes post-training alignment. This anchors the distinction between scaled pretraining and capabilities of a complete deployed system; it does not independently settle AGI.

evidence.excerpt: fails on some very easy tasks
evidence.explanation: The evaluator recognizes a substantial breakthrough but does not regard o3 as AGI. Because this was a system using additional computation at use time, its results are context rather than a direct test of pure pretraining.

This is material competing evidence: the authors describe broad capabilities and characterize GPT-4 as an early, incomplete AGI. Their qualified interpretation does not establish the broad human-level standard used here, but shows why 'clearly' is stronger than the consensus warrants.
